subject: Copywriting
title: Why Headlines Matter Most
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Why Headlines Matter Most.

hook.text: David Ogilvy said: 'Five times as many people read the headline as the body copy.' 80% of your work is the title.

buildup.text: A bad headline kills great copy. A great headline saves mediocre copy. The headline is the gatekeeper.

discovery.text: Ogilvy spent weeks on headlines. He wrote 104 versions for a single Rolls-Royce ad before choosing one.

twist.text: Most writers spend 5% of their time on headlines. The pros spend 50%. The ratio is backwards.

climax.text: The headline decides if anyone reads your work. Everything else is conditional on those first few words.

punchline.text: 80% of readers stop at the headline. Make it count.

quiz.question: According to Ogilvy, how many people only read the headline?

details.summary: David Ogilvy estimated that five times more people read headlines than body copy, meaning 80 cents of every advertising dollar is spent in the headline. A great headline can sell a mediocre product; a weak headline dooms even the best copy beneath it.
details.whyItMatters: If the headline fails, nothing else matters. This foundational truth applies to ads, emails, blog posts, and social media — making headline craft the single most valuable writing skill.
takeaways: Five times more people read headlines than body copy
Ogilvy called the headline 80 cents of every advertising dollar
Headline testing produces the largest performance gains in any copy

faq.question: Why do headlines matter more than body copy?
faq.answer: Most readers scan and never read beyond the headline. If the headline doesn't capture attention and promise value, the body copy — no matter how brilliant — is never seen. The headline is the ad for the rest of the ad.

faq.question: Does the headline rule apply beyond traditional advertising?
faq.answer: Absolutely. Blog post titles, email subject lines, social media hooks, and video thumbnails all function as headlines. Any content that competes for attention follows the same principle: the first line must earn the next.
